claims.text: The initial as-cast high-entropy alloy is homogeneous.
The initial alloy has a primarily single-phase microstructure.
High-temperature homogenization allows solute mixing in the alloy.
Rapid quenching followed by low-temperature aging promotes controlled nanoscale precipitate formation.
The multi-step heat treatment creates subtle compositional gradients at grain boundaries.
Nanoscale precipitates and grain-boundary compositional gradients act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Impeded dislocation motion increases Young's modulus.
Nanoscale secondary phases promote crack deflection and thereby improve fracture resistance.
Nanoscale secondary phases promote plasticity-induced toughening that enhances ductility.
Nanoscale secondary phases promote plasticity-induced toughening that enhances fracture resistance.
The proposed treatment will increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional homogenization.
The proposed treatment will increase ductility by approximately 15–30% relative to conventional homogenization.
The proposed treatment will increase Young's modulus by approximately 5–10% relative to conventional homogenization.
The proposed treatment will increase fracture resistance by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional homogenization.
The treatment is expected to work when the alloy composition supports multiple competing phases.
The treatment may not work when the alloy composition strongly favors a single phase.
Poorly controlled thermal gradients or processing parameters can prevent the proposed improvements.
Precipitate coarsening or formation of brittle secondary phases limits the effectiveness of the treatment.
The magnitude and scalability of the improvements vary with alloy composition and processing parameters.
